Triggers.value: A specific taste associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: control eating strictly to feel in control
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

issues.item: Triggers: Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me
issues.explanation: The trigger profile is dominated by interpersonal closeness plus taste and crying. For torture, gustatory and affective-expression triggers are plausible, but emotional closeness as a primary trigger is less well integrated with the rest of the profile, which contains no interpersonal betrayal/shame/relationship-based appraisals or memories to explain why closeness itself would be a salient cue. This creates a cross-node mismatch rather than a direct impossibility.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the formulation. The strongest active pathways involve triggers, negative appraisals, memory, and threat, but the other selected strategies are control/safety based (restrict eating, hypervigilance), whereas gambling is a sensation-seeking/distracting behavior with no support from the memory, threat, or appraisal items. It reads like a separate coping pattern rather than part of the same PTSD-maintaining loop.

'Concentration' is not a threat belief/state in the same way as the other threat items. 'Cannot Trust Safety' and 'Body Reacts Before Mind' reflect ongoing sense of current threat, but concentration difficulty is a nonspecific cognitive symptom and does not cohere tightly within the Threat node. Given the formulation emphasizes Memory → Threat and Maladaptive Strategies → Threat, a more direct threat-related item would be expected.

vignette:
Priya Subramaniam is a 47-year-old South Asian woman, divorced, who serves as a pastor at a small interfaith congregation in the mid-Atlantic region. She came to the clinic after more than two years of what she described, haltingly, as "not being myself anymore" - a phrase she returned to several times across the intake session, each time with the same flat, bewildered expression.

Approximately three years ago, Priya was detained during a humanitarian mission abroad. Over the course of several days, she was subjected to systematic torture by individuals who appeared to be affiliated with a paramilitary faction operating in the region. Among the methods used against her was forced ingestion of substances - contaminated water and spoiled food administered as both punishment and humiliation, accompanied by prolonged interrogation during which she was made to speak, repeatedly, about her identity, her faith, and her associations. She was eventually released, the circumstances of which remain, in her own account, genuinely unclear to her. She returned to the United States physically depleted and, in her words, "hollowed out."

In the months that followed, Priya noticed that certain ordinary moments would fracture without warning. The taste of anything bitter or metallic - a particular herbal tea she had once loved, certain tinned foods - would produce an immediate, overwhelming response that seemed to bypass any conscious recognition. She had come to believe that her body simply knew things her mind had not yet processed, that some animal part of her was still scanning for what came next. This sense of her own physiology as ungovernable had become one of the most frightening aspects of her daily experience. She was certain, in those moments, that she was not safe - and no reassurance from colleagues, her adult daughter, or her physician had been able to touch that certainty. When people told her she was home, that it was over, she understood the words but could not feel their truth.

Her memories of the detention itself arrive in a way she struggles to describe: some moments are almost unbearably vivid - the texture of a particular surface, a specific phrase repeated at her - while others are simply absent, blank stretches she cannot account for. The fragments do not assemble into a coherent sequence. When she does recall what she can, she is overtaken by guilt so acute it is almost physical, a conviction that she failed in ways she cannot fully articulate but cannot dismiss.

Priya has come to avoid several things with a consistency that has quietly restructured her life. She eats very little and controls what she eats with rigid precision - not out of any stated concern about weight, but because the act of choosing exactly what enters her body is one of the few domains in which she feels any agency. She has stopped drinking tea entirely. She does not speak about what happened to her, and when pastoral conversations with congregants have moved toward suffering, captivity, or loss, she has found reasons to redirect or conclude the session. She works hard, she said, not to think about it at all - a project that consumes enormous energy and that she knows, on some level, is not working.

The occupational consequences have accumulated. Priya's role requires her to be emotionally present, to sit with people in their grief, to offer homilies that draw on her own spiritual journey. She has delivered fewer sermons in the past eighteen months. She has delegated more. Several congregants have gently noted that she seems "elsewhere." She scans every new face that enters the sanctuary, watching for something she cannot name but recognises as threat. She had come to believe that the person she was - the pastor, the one who could hold other people's pain - no longer existed, and that what remained was a diminished version who had no particular future to move toward.

What finally brought her to seek help was a funeral service two months ago, during which she began to cry unexpectedly and could not stop. Crying had become, for her, one of the most destabilising experiences she knew - she associated it directly with those days of detention, when she had wept and it had been used against her. Afterward, she sat alone in the vestry for an hour. She came to therapy, she said, not because she believed it would work, but because she could no longer afford not to try.
